claims.text: Maintaining a chromium-rich passive film enhances the corrosion resistance of austenitic stainless steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Small additions of Mo and Nb promote the formation of Mo- and Nb-rich carbide precipitates.
Mo- and Nb-rich carbide precipitates sequester carbon.
Carbon sequestration by Mo- and Nb-rich carbides prevents deleterious chromium-carbide formation at grain boundaries.
Tailored heat treatments induce grain-boundary segregation of chromium and molybdenum.
Chromium and molybdenum segregation at grain boundaries reinforces the passive film at critical corrosion sites.
Standard AISI 316 stainless steel provides a representative initial state for the proposed study.
Intermediate-temperature annealing followed by rapid quenching can promote both bulk carbide precipitation and chromium/molybdenum grain-boundary segregation in micro-alloyed 316 stainless steel.
Chloride-rich electrolytes represent chemical-processing corrosion conditions.
Controlled humidity and moderate-temperature exposures represent relevant nuclear-power application conditions.
Carbide precipitates restrict carbon diffusion that would otherwise drive chromium-carbide formation and grain-boundary sensitization.
Heat-treatment-induced segregation increases local chromium and molybdenum concentrations along grain boundaries.
The combined carbide and segregation mechanisms stabilize a robust chromium-rich passive film.
A stabilized chromium-rich passive film mitigates pitting and intergranular corrosion.
Combined Mo/Nb micro-alloying and tailored heat treatment will improve corrosion resistance relative to baseline AISI 316.
The treated steel will show a lower pitting-initiation frequency than baseline AISI 316.
The treated steel will show greater passive-film stability than baseline AISI 316.
The magnitude of corrosion-resistance improvement depends on processing parameters, micro-alloying efficiency, and grain-boundary segregation kinetics.
The hypothesis is expected to apply under chloride-rich and moderate-temperature/humidity conditions but may fail under more extreme corrosive or thermal conditions.
The study will compare intervention and baseline samples using identical corrosion protocols while measuring pitting, passive-film response, carbide populations, and grain-boundary composition.
